meta_desc: Master class 5 maths basic operations on large numbers, learn which operation each situation needs, and solve real-life case studies. Free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: By Class 5 the four operations are not the hard part — deciding which one a word problem needs is. Here is how to read a real-life situation, pick add, subtract, multiply or divide, and solve multi-step problems, with two worked case studies and a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Give a Class 5 student the sum 4,275 × 6 and most will get it right. Hand the same child a paragraph about a school buying 6 cartons of 4,275 notebooks and ask ‘how many notebooks in all?’ and suddenly a third of the class freezes. That gap is the whole story of class 5 maths basic operations. The arithmetic — addition, subtraction, multiplication and division on large numbers — is usually solid by now. The skill that separates a confident Class 5 student from a shaky one is reading a real situation and deciding which operation it actually needs.

In my experience teaching ten-year-olds, the drills are rarely the problem. The problem is the moment a child meets three sentences of context, a couple of numbers in the thousands, and no operation sign telling them what to do. So this guide spends less time on how to carry and borrow, and more on how to choose.

The four operations and the situations that signal them

Each operation answers a particular kind of question. Once a child learns to match the situation to the operation, word problems stop being guesswork. Here is the mapping I drill until it is automatic.

OperationUse it when the situation is…Everyday signal wordsExample
AdditionCombining amounts, finding a totalin all, altogether, sum, bothSales of ₹12,400 and ₹9,850
SubtractionTaking away, finding a difference or what is leftleft, remaining, how much more, fewerHad ₹20,000, spent ₹13,600
MultiplicationEqual groups repeatedeach, per, times, rows of8 boxes of 145 tiles each
DivisionSharing equally or making equal groupseach, split, shared, per, distributed1,260 pencils into 35 boxes

Notice the trap in that table: ‘each’ and ‘per’ show up under both multiplication and division. This is the single most common mistake I see. Signal words are a hint, never a rule. ‘8 boxes of 145 tiles each’ multiplies; ‘1,260 pencils shared into boxes of 35 each’ divides. The child has to picture the situation, not just scan for a keyword.

A four-step method for any word problem

When a Class 5 student is stuck, it is almost always because they jumped straight to calculating. Slow the first thirty seconds down with these four steps:

  • What is being asked? Underline the actual question. Is it a total, a difference, a product, or a share?
  • What do I know? List the numbers and their units (rupees, students, litres).
  • Which operation fits? Match the situation to the table above — combine, take away, repeat equal groups, or share equally.
  • Does the answer make sense? Estimate first. If you divide 1,260 by 35 and get 4,200, something is wrong.

That last step is the one children skip and the one that catches the most errors. Rounding 4,275 × 6 to 4,000 × 6 = 24,000 tells you instantly whether a slipped digit has thrown your answer off by a factor of ten.

Working with large numbers cleanly

Class 5 pushes the numbers into the thousands and beyond, so neat place-value alignment matters more than ever. A few habits that pay off:

  • Line up digits by place value — ones under ones, thousands under thousands — before you add or subtract.
  • In long multiplication, write a 0 as a placeholder when you move to the tens row. Missing placeholders cause more wrong answers at this level than any actual multiplication error.
  • In long division, check with the rule dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder. It is the cheapest self-check there is.

Case study 1: the school stationery order

Here is the kind of passage the Class 5 exam now favours — and exactly what our case-study e-book is built around. Read it, then decide the operations before you calculate.

Sunrise Public School ordered 8 cartons of exercise books. Each carton holds 375 books. The school already had 1,240 books in the store. During the year, students used 6,500 books.

Question 1: How many books did the school buy? Equal groups repeated — that is multiplication. 375 × 8 = 3,000 books.

Question 2: How many books did the school have in total? Combine the new books with the old stock — addition. 3,000 + 1,240 = 4,240 books.

Question 3: How many books were left at the end of the year? Take away what was used — subtraction. 4,240 − 6,500 is not possible; the store did not have enough, so it must have reordered. This is a genuine multi-step problem where the ‘obvious’ subtraction reveals something about the situation. Good problems do that.

Case study 2: sharing the trip cost

A Class 5 trip cost ₹42,000 in total. There were 35 students, and each student also paid ₹150 for lunch on top of the shared cost.

Question 1: What was the shared cost per student? Sharing equally — division. 42,000 ÷ 35 = ₹1,200 each.

Question 2: What did each student pay altogether? Combine the share with lunch — addition. 1,200 + 150 = ₹1,350.

Question 3: What did all 35 students pay in total? Equal groups — multiplication. 1,350 × 35 = ₹47,250. Cross-check: 42,000 shared cost + (150 × 35 = 5,250 lunch) = 47,250. The two routes agree, so the answer holds.

That cross-check is worth teaching as a habit. When a multi-step problem can be solved two ways and both land on the same number, a child stops second-guessing and starts trusting their own working.

One honest caveat

Do not let a child memorise signal words as a shortcut. I have watched students see the word ‘each’ and multiply on autopilot when the problem clearly asked them to share. Keyword-spotting works until an exam writer deliberately breaks it — and Class 5 papers increasingly do. Understanding beats pattern-matching every single time.

quiz.title: Class 5 Basic Operations Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing large numbers, plus choosing the right operation for a real situation. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Class 5 four basic operations on large numbers

questions.q: A shop earned ₹18,650 on Monday and ₹21,470 on Tuesday. How much in all?
A tank held 9,000 litres. 3,750 litres were used. How much is left?
questions.explanation: ‘Left’ means take away, so subtract: 9,000 − 3,750 = 5,250 litres.

questions.q: A factory makes 1,250 bottles each day. How many in 6 days?
questions.explanation: Equal groups repeated is multiplication: 1,250 × 6 = 7,500 bottles.

questions.q: 1,260 pencils are packed equally into 35 boxes. How many per box?
questions.explanation: Sharing equally is division: 1,260 ÷ 35 = 36 pencils per box.

questions.q: Which operation should you use for: ‘8 shelves hold 145 books each. How many books in all?’
questions.explanation: Equal groups (145 repeated 8 times) means multiply: 145 × 8 = 1,160.

questions.q: A trip cost ₹42,000 shared equally among 35 students. What is each share?
A school bought 8 cartons of 375 books, then added them to 1,240 books in store. How many now?
questions.explanation: First multiply: 375 × 8 = 3,000. Then add the stock: 3,000 + 1,240 = 4,240 books.

questions.q: Estimate 4,275 × 6 by rounding to the nearest thousand first.
questions.explanation: Round 4,275 to 4,000, then 4,000 × 6 = 24,000 — a quick check that the exact answer, 25,650, is sensible.

faq.q: What are the four basic operations in Class 5 maths?
faq.a: Addition, subtraction, multiplication and division. In Class 5 they are applied to large numbers — often four and five digits — and combined in multi-step word problems rather than done in isolation.

faq.q: How does my child know which operation a word problem needs?
faq.a: Teach the situation, not just keywords: combine amounts means add, find what is left means subtract, repeat equal groups means multiply, and share equally means divide. Signal words like ‘each’ are hints, not rules — the child must picture what is happening.

faq.q: Why does my child get calculations right but fail word problems?
faq.a: Because word problems test a second skill — reading a situation and choosing the operation — on top of the arithmetic. Practising with real-life case studies, where the passage does not tell you which operation to use, closes that gap faster than more sums.

faq.q: What is a multi-step problem in Class 5?
faq.a: A problem that needs two or more operations in order — for example multiply to find a total, then subtract what was used. The trick is to answer one small question at a time and check that each step makes sense before moving on.
